name: Hindsight Bias
description: After learning an outcome, people overestimate how predictable it was and misremember what they believed beforehand. The past starts to feel more obvious than it actually was at the time.
design_relevance_note: Matters in retrospective product reviews, incident analysis, usability-test interpretation, experiment readouts, and any workflow where teams may unfairly judge earlier decisions as 'obviously' right or wrong after seeing the result.
prevalence_note: A classic judgment-and-decision bias taught across psychology and behavioral-economics curricula, and directly relevant to product retrospectives and research debriefs.

findings.description: Across three experiments, learning an outcome made people judge that outcome as having been more likely all along, changed which evidence they saw as relevant, and led them to overestimate what they or others would have known without outcome knowledge. Participants were largely unaware of the distortion — the core hindsight-bias pattern.
findings.source_title: Hindsight is not equal to foresight: The effect of outcome knowledge on judgment under uncertainty.
findings.source_venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance

applications.title: 705 failed startup founders misremembering their own pre-failure confidence
applications.description: A survey of 705 entrepreneurs whose startups had failed found that 77.3% had believed, before failure, that their venture would grow into a successful, cash-flow-positive business -- but after the failure, only 58% recalled having originally believed that, a real-time gap between contemporaneously-recorded confidence and later-recalled confidence.
applications.ethical_note: A real-world illustration of hindsight bias distorting entrepreneurs' own self-assessment after failure, not a designed influence on a user -- directly relevant to any product-analytics or retrospective process (post-mortems, churn analysis) where people are asked to recall their own prior confidence or expectations after an outcome is already known.

applications.title: Predicting Clarence Thomas's Senate confirmation: a hindsight-bias study
applications.description: In a 1993 study, researchers Dorothee Dietrich and Matthew Olson asked 57 college students at Hamline University to predict, before the vote, whether the U.S. Senate would confirm Supreme Court nominee Clarence Thomas. Beforehand, 58% predicted he would be confirmed. A month after his actual confirmation, when asked to recall their prediction, 78% of the same participants claimed they had correctly predicted the outcome -- a 20-percentage-point jump in self-reported accuracy consistent with hindsight bias.
applications.ethical_note: This documents a real, quantified academic study tied to a specific, verifiable historical event, not a persuasion or product-design case. Included to ground Hindsight Bias in a concrete, dated instance rather than leaving it purely theoretical, consistent with how other classical-bias entries in this corpus (Base Rate Fallacy, Gambler's Fallacy) are handled in this same wave.

applications.title: The 'worst call in Super Bowl history': judging a decision by its outcome, not its odds
applications.description: After Seattle Seahawks coach Pete Carroll called a goal-line pass play (rather than a run) that was intercepted to end Super Bowl XLIX, the Seattle Times and other outlets immediately labeled it 'the worst call in Super Bowl history' -- even though, at the time the decision was made, the play call was a defensible one given the game situation, and the outcome (an interception) was far from the most likely result.
applications.ethical_note: A real-time public illustration of hindsight bias, not a designed influence on a user -- directly relevant to how product/design decisions get judged after the fact: a reasonable decision that happens to produce a bad outcome (an A/B test variant that underperforms despite sound reasoning, a feature bet that doesn't pay off) is easy to mislabel as an obviously bad call in hindsight, when it may have been a defensible decision under the uncertainty that existed at the time.
